subject: selective
title: Reading comprehension · Test 3
summary: A 30-minute practice reading test with four original passages (including a poem) and 30 multiple-choice questions on main idea, inference, vocabulary, tone and poetry.
body:
Read the four passages below, then answer the 30 questions. You have 30 minutes. Each question names the passage it is about. Look back at the passage for every answer — the evidence is always there in the text.

## Passage A — Where to Look

Ava had practised in the school pool a dozen times. She knew how to clear her mask, how to breathe slowly through the snorkel, how to float face-down like a starfish. None of that seemed to matter now that the real ocean was slapping against the side of the boat.

"Buddies, hold hands," called Mr Delaney. Ava's buddy was Jonah, who talked too much and was afraid of nothing. He was already sitting on the edge of the boat with his flippers on the wrong feet.

The water was colder than the pool and much, much bigger. When Ava lowered her face in, she saw nothing at first but blue — a deep, endless blue that went down and down with no floor. Her chest tightened. She lifted her head, gasping, and her mask filled with water.

"You right?" Jonah said, bobbing beside her.

"Fine," she lied.

She wanted to swim straight back to the ladder. Instead she remembered the instructor's words from the pool: when you panic, do the next small thing. Not the whole thing. Just the next small thing.

So she cleared her mask. That was one small thing. She put the snorkel back in her mouth. Another. She breathed in for four counts and out for four. Another. Jonah, for once, said nothing. He just held her hand and waited.

When she put her face back in the water, she looked along the reef instead of down. And there, right below her, was a whole street of life. A school of tiny silver fish turned all at once, like a single flashing coin. A parrotfish crunched at the coral, loud enough to hear. Something blue and frilly opened and closed in a crack in the rock.

Ava forgot to be afraid. She forgot, for nearly a minute, to breathe in fours. She pointed and Jonah pointed back, and they had a whole conversation without a single word.

Back on the boat, Mr Delaney asked if anyone had found it difficult.

Ava thought about it. "At first," she said. "Then I worked out where to look."

## Passage B — Reading the Rings

A tree trunk is a kind of diary. Cut across it and you will see a pattern of circles, one inside the other, spreading out from the centre like ripples on a pond. Each of these growth rings can tell a story about one year in the tree's life.

In places with clear seasons, a tree grows quickly in spring and early summer, when there is plenty of water and sunlight. This wood is pale and soft. Later in the year growth slows, and the wood that forms is darker and denser. Together, one pale band and one dark band make up a single year's ring. Counting the rings from the bark to the centre gives the tree's age.

The rings do more than count years. In a wet, warm year, a tree grows a wide ring. In a year of drought, the ring may be so thin it is hard to see. A fire can leave a black scar, and an insect attack can leave a ring that is narrow or damaged. Scientists who study tree rings are called dendrochronologists, from Greek words meaning "tree", "time" and "study".

Because nearby trees of the same kind live through the same weather, they share the same pattern of wide and narrow rings, a little like a barcode. This lets scientists match a living tree with an old wooden beam or a log buried in a swamp. By overlapping patterns from older and older wood, they have built records stretching back thousands of years. These records help to date old buildings and show how the climate has changed over time.

Tree-ring dating does have limits. In places without a strong change of seasons, such as some tropical areas, trees may not form clear yearly rings at all. In very dry years, some trees can skip a ring entirely, and now and then a tree forms two rings in one year after an unusual season. That is why scientists never rely on a single tree; they compare many.

Scientists do not even need to cut a tree down. They can use a thin, hollow drill to remove a pencil-sized core of wood, and the tree survives.

The next time you walk past a stump, take a closer look. You may be reading a history book written in wood.

## Passage C — Kite

It sulked all winter in the shed,  
a heap of sticks and tangled thread,  
its paper face torn at the chin,  
too tired to let the daylight in.

But Saturday the north wind came  
and called the old kite by its name;  
we carried it up Tower Hill  
where even the grass would not keep still.

I ran. It dragged. I ran again.  
It scraped the ground, and then — and then —  
it caught the wind, it tugged, it rose,  
it climbed above my upturned nose.

And now it bucks against the string  
like something wild, a living thing,  
and I, who thought I held it fast,  
am being held by it at last.

## Passage D — Why I Still Write Letters

My friends think I am strange. In a world of instant messages, I write letters — on paper, with a pen, in envelopes with stamps. I post one most weeks. And I want to convince you to try it.

A message on a phone takes seconds to send and, too often, seconds to forget. A letter takes time to write, and that is exactly the point. When you know you can't delete and retype endlessly, you think harder about what you really want to say. Your words become slower, but also more honest.

Then there is the waiting. People say this is the worst thing about letters, but I disagree. Waiting for a reply turns it into an event. I have a shoebox of letters from my cousin in Darwin, and I can remember where I was standing when I opened almost every one of them. I cannot say the same about a single text message.

Letters are also something you can keep and hold. Handwriting carries a person in a way a screen font never can: the way my grandmother crosses her sevens, the coffee ring on a page from my cousin, the doodle in the corner.

I am not saying we should throw away our phones. I use mine every day, and a quick message is perfect for "running late" or "what's the homework?". But for the things that matter — thank you, I'm sorry, I miss you — a letter says something a text cannot: you were worth my time.

So find a pen. Choose one person. Write them a page. You might be surprised by what comes back.

— Lena Hart, aged 13

questions.prompt: In Passage A, when Jonah asks if she is all right, Ava says "Fine" — but the writer adds 'she lied'. What does this show?

options.A: Ava is feeling completely calm.
options.B: Ava is more frightened than she wants Jonah to know.
options.C: Ava is angry with Jonah for bothering her.
options.D: Ava did not hear Jonah's question properly.

questions.explanation: She has just panicked (chest tight, gasping, mask flooded), so saying 'Fine' is hiding her fear. The word 'lied' rules out 'completely calm'.
steps: Look at what happened just before: her chest tightened, she gasped, her mask filled with water.
The writer says her 'Fine' was a lie, so she was not fine.
So she is hiding how frightened she is.

mistakes.A: Trap: believing the character instead of the narrator. The writer tells us her answer was a lie.
mistakes.C: Trap: inventing a feeling. Nothing shows anger — she has just been gasping in fright.
mistakes.D: Trap: missing that she answered. She heard him and chose to hide the truth.

questions.prompt: In Passage A, the school of fish 'turned all at once, like a single flashing coin'. This comparison shows that the fish

options.A: moved together at the same moment, catching the light
options.B: were gold in colour
options.C: were rare and valuable
options.D: scattered in different directions

questions.explanation: 'All at once' and 'a single … coin' show the whole school moving as one, and 'flashing' shows the silver catching light. The fish are silver, so 'gold' is wrong.
steps: Find the key words: 'all at once', 'single', 'flashing'.
Many fish acting like ONE coin means they moved together; 'flashing' means they shone.
So the fish moved together at the same moment, catching the light.

mistakes.B: Trap: picturing a gold coin. The fish are described as 'silver'.
mistakes.C: Trap: taking the money idea too far. The comparison is about how they moved and shone.
mistakes.D: Trap: the opposite. 'All at once' and 'single' mean they moved as one.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of Passage A?

options.A: Jonah is a careless student who cannot put his flippers on properly.
options.B: By taking small steps, Ava gets past her fear and discovers something wonderful.
options.C: Snorkelling in the open ocean is far too dangerous for school students to try at all.
options.D: Pool practice turns out to be a waste of time.

questions.explanation: Ava panics, uses the 'next small thing' advice, and then sees the reef full of life — fear overcome, wonder found. The pool advice helps her, so pool practice was not wasted.
steps: Trace Ava's journey: panic, then small steps, then wonder at the reef.
The turning point is 'do the next small thing'.
So the main idea is that small steps help her overcome fear and discover something wonderful.

mistakes.A: Trap: a small detail about another character. The story is about Ava's experience.
mistakes.C: Trap: a big claim the story does not make. Ava ends up enjoying it and nobody is hurt.
mistakes.D: Trap: the opposite. The instructor's advice from the pool is what helps her.

questions.prompt: In Passage A, why does Jonah, 'for once', say nothing?

options.A: He is too frightened of the deep water to speak.
options.B: He realises Ava is struggling and gives her quiet support.
options.C: He is annoyed with Ava for slowing him down.
options.D: He has swum off to look at the reef by himself.

questions.explanation: Jonah usually 'talked too much', so staying silent while holding her hand shows he understands she needs calm. He is 'afraid of nothing', so fear is not the reason.
steps: Remember Jonah's character: he 'talked too much' — so silence is unusual.
He 'just held her hand and waited' while Ava calmed herself.
So he stays quiet to support her because he sees she is struggling.

mistakes.A: Trap: ignoring his character. Jonah is described as 'afraid of nothing'.
mistakes.C: Trap: inventing a feeling. He holds her hand and waits, which is kind, not annoyed.
mistakes.D: Trap: missing a detail. He 'held her hand and waited' beside her.

questions.prompt: In Passage A, what made the biggest difference the second time Ava put her face in the water?

options.A: Mr Delaney swam over to help her.
options.B: Jonah lent her a better mask.
options.C: She looked along the reef instead of down into the deep water.
options.D: The water became warmer.

questions.explanation: The passage says 'she looked along the reef instead of down' and found 'a whole street of life'. The first time she looked down into endless blue. No one gave her new equipment.
steps: Compare the two times: first she saw 'endless blue' going down; second she 'looked along the reef instead of down'.
Looking along the reef showed her the fish and coral.
So the difference was where she looked: along the reef, not down.

mistakes.A: Trap: inventing help. Mr Delaney only speaks on the boat.
mistakes.B: Trap: inventing a detail. She cleared her own mask.
mistakes.D: Trap: inventing a change. The water is never described as getting warmer.

questions.prompt: Ava's last words in Passage A are "Then I worked out where to look." Which is the best interpretation?

options.A: Choosing what to focus on helped her handle her fear, not just find the fish.
options.B: She means only that she found the best spot on the reef to see the most fish.
options.C: She is blaming Mr Delaney for not telling her where to look.
options.D: She is admitting that she never saw anything interesting.

questions.explanation: Mr Delaney asks if it was difficult; her answer explains how she beat the difficulty — by focusing on the reef instead of the frightening depth, and on small steps instead of the whole thing. The literal meaning alone misses the link to her fear.
steps: Note the question she is answering: did anyone find it 'difficult'?
Looking down into the depth caused her panic; looking along the reef brought wonder.
So her line means that choosing what to focus on helped her manage her fear.

mistakes.B: Trap: stopping at the surface meaning. It is literally true, but she is answering a question about finding it difficult.
mistakes.C: Trap: inventing blame. Her tone is thoughtful, not complaining.
mistakes.D: Trap: contradicting the story. She saw silver fish, a parrotfish and more.

questions.prompt: In Passage A, 'Her chest tightened.' This suggests Ava

options.A: was wearing a wetsuit that was too small
options.B: felt a sudden rush of fear
options.C: was taking a deep, relaxed breath
options.D: was getting ready to dive deeper

questions.explanation: It happens as she sees the endless blue, and next she gasps and lifts her head — a body reacting to fear. Nothing about clothing is mentioned.
steps: Look at what she has just seen: 'a deep, endless blue … with no floor'.
Look at what happens next: she lifts her head, gasping.
So her chest tightening shows a sudden rush of fear.

mistakes.A: Trap: reading it literally. No wetsuit is mentioned; this describes a feeling.
mistakes.C: Trap: the opposite. She lifts her head 'gasping' straight after.
mistakes.D: Trap: missing what she does next. She lifts her head out of the water.

questions.prompt: How does the writer of Passage A use the description of the ocean to show the change in Ava?

options.A: The ocean first seems empty and endless, then becomes a busy 'street of life', matching her change from fear to wonder.
options.B: The ocean is always described as dangerous, showing Ava never relaxes.
options.C: The writer shows the weather becoming calmer during the swim.
options.D: The ocean is compared to the school pool all the way through, to show that Ava's practice made the real ocean feel exactly the same.

questions.explanation: First: 'nothing … but blue … no floor' (empty, scary). Later: 'a whole street of life' (busy, friendly). The setting changes as Ava's feelings change. She clearly relaxes, so 'never relaxes' is wrong.
steps: Find the first description: 'nothing at first but blue … with no floor' — empty and frightening.
Find the second: 'a whole street of life' — busy and welcoming.
The change in the ocean's description mirrors Ava's change from fear to wonder.

mistakes.B: Trap: reading only the first half. Later the reef is full of life and she 'forgot to be afraid'.
mistakes.C: Trap: inventing a detail. The weather is not described changing.
mistakes.D: Trap: the opposite. The ocean is 'colder' and 'much, much bigger' than the pool.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of Passage B, 'Reading the Rings'?

options.A: To persuade people to stop cutting down trees, since scientists can study them without doing so
options.B: To explain how tree rings record a tree's age and history, and how scientists use them
options.C: To tell the story of one particular old tree
options.D: To teach readers how to drill into trees at home

questions.explanation: Each paragraph explains something about rings — how they form, what they show, how they are matched, their limits. It does not argue, so it is not persuasive.
steps: List the paragraphs: how rings form, what they show, matching patterns, limits, the drill.
All explain; none argue.
So the purpose is to explain how tree rings record age and history and how scientists use them.

mistakes.A: Trap: over-reading one line. The passage mentions not needing to cut trees, but it never argues for anything.
mistakes.C: Trap: wrong text type. No single tree is followed; the passage explains rings in general.
mistakes.D: Trap: choosing a small detail. The drill is mentioned in one short paragraph about scientists.

questions.prompt: According to Passage B, what does a very thin tree ring usually show?

options.A: A year with plenty of rain
options.B: A forest fire
options.C: The tree's very first year
options.D: A year of drought or poor growing conditions

questions.explanation: The passage says 'In a year of drought, the ring may be so thin it is hard to see.' Wet years give wide rings, the opposite.
steps: Find the paragraph about what rings show.
'In a year of drought, the ring may be so thin it is hard to see.'
So a very thin ring usually shows a drought or poor growing year.

mistakes.A: Trap: reversing the rule. A wet, warm year gives a wide ring.
mistakes.B: Trap: mixing up the clues. A fire leaves a black scar.
mistakes.C: Trap: guessing. The passage never links thin rings to a tree's first year.

questions.prompt: Passage B says 'dendrochronologists' comes from Greek words meaning 'tree', 'time' and 'study'. Which part of the word most likely means 'time'?

options.A: dendro
options.B: log
options.C: chrono
options.D: ist

questions.explanation: The meanings are listed in the same order as the word parts: dendro (tree) + chrono (time) + logist (study). 'Chrono' also appears in 'chronological' (in time order). 'Log' is tempting because of wooden logs, but here it means study.
steps: Split the word: dendro + chrono + log + ist.
Match in order: tree, time, study (+ '-ist', a person who does it).
So 'chrono' means time.

mistakes.A: Trap: matching the first part to the wrong meaning. The words are listed in order — tree, time, study — so the first part means 'tree'.
mistakes.B: Trap: thinking of a wooden log. In this word, '-log-' belongs to the 'study' part, as in 'biology'.
mistakes.D: Trap: picking the ending. '-ist' just means a person who does something, like 'artist'.

questions.prompt: A cut log shows 48 pale bands and 48 dark bands. Using Passage B, about how old was the tree?

options.A: About 48 years old
options.B: About 96 years old
options.C: About 24 years old
options.D: About 49 years old

questions.explanation: One pale band plus one dark band = one year, so 48 pairs = 48 years. Counting all 96 bands double-counts each year.
steps: The passage: 'one pale band and one dark band make up a single year's ring.'
48 pale + 48 dark = 48 pairs.
So the tree was about 48 years old.

mistakes.B: Trap: counting every band as a year. The passage says one pale band AND one dark band make one year's ring.
mistakes.C: Trap: dividing twice. 48 pairs of bands already gives the number of years; don't halve it again.
mistakes.D: Trap: adding one for no reason. Each pale-and-dark pair is one year, so the pairs are the years.

questions.prompt: In Passage B, why does the writer compare tree-ring patterns to 'a barcode'?

options.A: To suggest that wood is sold in supermarkets
options.B: To show that tree rings are black and white stripes, just like the lines on a product's barcode
options.C: To say that scientists print patterns onto trees
options.D: To show that a pattern of wide and narrow rings can be recognised and matched, like a code

questions.explanation: A barcode is a pattern of thick and thin lines that can be scanned and matched; tree rings are a pattern of wide and narrow rings that scientists match between trees and beams. The colour idea is tempting but misses the point.
steps: What is a barcode? A pattern of thick and thin lines that identifies something.
The passage then explains matching a living tree with an old beam using the shared pattern.
So the comparison shows the pattern can be recognised and matched like a code.

mistakes.A: Trap: thinking about where barcodes are found. The comparison is about the pattern, not shopping.
mistakes.B: Trap: matching the colours. Rings are pale and dark, but the point is the wide-and-narrow pattern.
mistakes.C: Trap: reading it literally. The patterns grow naturally with the weather.

questions.prompt: Which statement would the writer of Passage B, 'Reading the Rings', most likely agree with?

options.A: Tree rings give a perfect, error-free record of every single year in every part of the world.
options.B: You can only see a tree's rings by cutting it down.
options.C: Tropical trees are always older than other trees.
options.D: Tree-ring dating is very useful, but it must be checked against many trees.

questions.explanation: The writer shows many uses (dating buildings, climate records) but says 'scientists never rely on a single tree; they compare many'. The 'limits' paragraph rules out a perfect record everywhere.
steps: The passage praises tree rings: they date buildings and show climate change.
But the limits paragraph ends: 'scientists never rely on a single tree; they compare many.'
So the writer would agree the method is useful but must be checked across many trees.

mistakes.A: Trap: missing the 'limits' paragraph. Some tropical trees have no clear rings, and rings can be skipped or doubled.
mistakes.B: Trap: missing a detail. A thin hollow drill takes a core and the tree survives.
mistakes.C: Trap: inventing a fact. The passage only says some tropical trees lack clear rings.

questions.prompt: In Passage B, which paragraph would best fit under the heading 'Problems with the method'?

options.A: The paragraph beginning 'In places with clear seasons'
options.B: The paragraph beginning 'Tree-ring dating does have limits'
options.C: The paragraph beginning 'Because nearby trees of the same kind'
options.D: The paragraph beginning 'Scientists do not even need to cut a tree down'

questions.explanation: That paragraph lists what can go wrong: no clear rings in some tropical areas, skipped rings, double rings. The 'clear seasons' paragraph explains how rings form, not problems.
steps: Look for a paragraph about things going wrong.
'Tree-ring dating does have limits' lists missing rings, skipped rings and double rings.
So that paragraph fits 'Problems with the method'.

mistakes.A: Trap: matching a single phrase. This paragraph explains how rings form; it doesn't list problems.
mistakes.C: Trap: choosing the matching method. This paragraph shows what works, not what goes wrong.
mistakes.D: Trap: mistaking a benefit for a problem. This paragraph describes an advantage of the method.

questions.prompt: The outermost ring of an old wooden beam from a farmhouse matches the ring that local trees grew in 1850. Based on Passage B, what does this most likely tell scientists?

options.A: The beam's tree was probably cut down in or soon after 1850, so the farmhouse was built no earlier than that.
options.B: The farmhouse was built exactly 1,850 years ago.
options.C: The beam's tree started growing in 1850, so the farmhouse must have been built many decades after that date.
options.D: The beam must come from a tree that is still alive today.

questions.explanation: The outermost ring is the last year the tree grew, so it was cut in or soon after 1850, and the house using it cannot be older than that. The first ring (the centre) would show when it started growing, not the outer ring.
steps: The outermost ring is the last ring the tree grew before it was cut.
It matches 1850, so the tree stopped growing in about 1850 — it was cut then or soon after.
So the farmhouse was built no earlier than about 1850.

mistakes.B: Trap: treating the year as a number of years. 1850 is a calendar year, not an age.
mistakes.C: Trap: mixing up inner and outer rings. The outermost ring is the last one grown, not the first.
mistakes.D: Trap: ignoring how beams are made. A tree cut into a beam stops growing; its last ring shows when it was cut.

questions.prompt: In Passage C, 'It sulked all winter in the shed' is an example of

options.A: a simile
options.B: onomatopoeia
options.C: a rhetorical question
options.D: personification

questions.explanation: Sulking is a human mood; giving it to a kite is personification. It isn't a simile because nothing is compared using 'like' or 'as'.
steps: Ask: who sulks? People do — it is a human mood.
Here a kite is said to sulk.
Giving a human quality to an object is personification.

mistakes.A: Trap: naming a comparison device. There is no 'like' or 'as' in this line.
mistakes.B: Trap: confusing devices. No word here imitates a sound.
mistakes.C: Trap: confusing devices. The line is a statement, not a question.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the rhyme pattern of Passage C?

options.A: The lines rhyme in pairs: lines 1 and 2, then lines 3 and 4.
options.B: Only the second and fourth lines of each stanza rhyme.
options.C: The poem does not rhyme at all.
options.D: The first and last lines of each stanza rhyme.

questions.explanation: Stanza 1 ends shed/thread, chin/in; stanza 4 ends string/thing, fast/last — rhyming couplets (AABB). 'Shed' and 'in' don't rhyme, so it isn't first-and-last.
steps: List the endings of stanza 1: shed, thread, chin, in.
shed/thread rhyme and chin/in rhyme; check stanza 4: string/thing, fast/last.
So the lines rhyme in pairs (couplets).

mistakes.B: Trap: not checking all the endings. 'Shed' rhymes with 'thread', lines 1 and 2.
mistakes.C: Trap: missing obvious rhymes. 'Rose' and 'nose' rhyme.
mistakes.D: Trap: checking the wrong lines. 'Shed' and 'in' do not rhyme.

questions.prompt: Why does the third stanza of Passage C begin with the short sentences 'I ran. It dragged. I ran again.'?

options.A: To show the speaker is bored with the kite
options.B: Because short sentences are needed to make the lines rhyme
options.C: To copy the stop-start effort of trying to get the kite into the air
options.D: To show the kite is broken beyond repair

questions.explanation: The choppy sentences mimic running, stopping and trying again, before the longer flowing lines when the kite finally rises. The kite flies, so it isn't broken beyond repair.
steps: Notice the rhythm: three very short sentences, each with a stop.
They describe running and dragging — repeated attempts.
So they copy the stop-start effort of launching the kite.

mistakes.A: Trap: misreading short sentences as dull. Here they show effort and struggle.
mistakes.B: Trap: mixing up rhyme and sentence length. Rhyme depends on line endings, not sentence length.
mistakes.D: Trap: ignoring what comes next. The kite rises a few lines later.

questions.prompt: In the last stanza of Passage C, the kite 'bucks against the string'. Here 'bucks' means it

options.A: jerks and pulls wildly, like a horse trying to throw off its rider
options.B: costs a lot of money
options.C: hangs still in the air
options.D: bends gently in the breeze

questions.explanation: A horse that 'bucks' kicks and jerks to break free; the next line calls the kite 'something wild, a living thing', so it is pulling hard against the string. The money meaning doesn't fit the sentence.
steps: Read the next line: 'like something wild, a living thing'.
A wild animal that 'bucks' jerks and kicks to get free — like a horse.
So 'bucks' means the kite jerks and pulls wildly against the string.

mistakes.B: Trap: a slang meaning of 'bucks' (dollars). That makes no sense with 'against the string'.
mistakes.C: Trap: the opposite. The next line calls it 'something wild'.
mistakes.D: Trap: too soft. 'Wild' and 'living thing' suggest strong, sudden movement.

questions.prompt: How does the kite change from the first stanza to the last stanza of Passage C?

options.A: From a brand-new, shiny toy into a broken one that is thrown back in the shed
options.B: From a flying kite to one stuck in a tree
options.C: It stays the same; only the weather changes
options.D: From a neglected, lifeless object to something that seems wild and alive

questions.explanation: In stanza 1 it 'sulked', is 'torn' and 'too tired'; in stanza 4 it 'bucks' 'like something wild, a living thing'. It was never new, so 'new to broken' reverses it.
steps: Stanza 1: the kite sulks, is torn and 'too tired' — neglected and lifeless.
Stanza 4: it 'bucks' like 'something wild, a living thing'.
So it changes from lifeless and neglected to wild and alive.

mistakes.A: Trap: reversing the order. It starts torn and tired, and ends flying.
mistakes.B: Trap: inventing an event. No tree appears in the poem.
mistakes.C: Trap: missing the change. It goes from 'too tired' to 'a living thing'.

questions.prompt: What do the last two lines of Passage C ('and I, who thought I held it fast, / am being held by it at last') most likely mean?

options.A: The kite pulls so strongly that it actually lifts the speaker off the ground and carries them along the hill.
options.B: The speaker's hand is tangled in the kite string by accident.
options.C: The speaker meant to control the kite, but is now completely caught up in the thrill of flying it.
options.D: The speaker has let go and the kite has flown away.

questions.explanation: The lines reverse who holds whom: the speaker thought they controlled the kite, but now the kite has captured their attention and joy. 'Lifted off the ground' takes the words too literally.
steps: Notice the reversal: 'I held it' becomes 'held by it'.
Being 'held' by something can mean being captivated by it.
So the speaker, meant to control the kite, is now captivated by the thrill of flying it.

mistakes.A: Trap: taking 'held' literally. The speaker is still on the hill; 'held' means gripped by the experience.
mistakes.B: Trap: inventing a problem. Nothing suggests an accident; the mood is joyful.
mistakes.D: Trap: contradicting the lines. The speaker still 'held it'; the kite is still pulling on the string.

questions.prompt: Which word best describes the speaker's mood at the end of Passage C?

options.A: Gloomy
options.B: Thrilled
options.C: Frightened
options.D: Bored

questions.explanation: The kite 'bucks' like 'something wild', and the speaker is 'held by it' — excited and absorbed, which is thrilled. 'Gloomy' fits only the opening stanza.
steps: Look at the final stanza's energy: 'bucks', 'wild', 'a living thing'.
The speaker is captivated — 'held by it at last'.
So the mood is thrilled.

mistakes.A: Trap: using the first stanza. Gloom belongs to the sulking kite in winter, not the ending.
mistakes.C: Trap: misreading 'wild'. The wildness is exciting, and the speaker is enjoying it.
mistakes.D: Trap: no evidence. Being 'held' by the kite shows the speaker is completely absorbed.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main argument in Passage D?

options.A: Phones should be banned for teenagers.
options.B: Postage stamps cost too much money.
options.C: Letters are a faster and more reliable way of reaching friends and family than text messages or emails.
options.D: Handwritten letters are worth writing because they are more thoughtful and lasting than quick messages.

questions.explanation: The writer argues letters make you think harder, are kept and treasured, and show someone 'was worth my time'. She keeps using her phone, so she is not arguing for a ban.
steps: Find the writer's request: 'I want to convince you to try it' (writing letters).
Her reasons: more thought, more honest, special to receive, something to keep.
So her argument is that letters are worth writing because they are more thoughtful and lasting.

mistakes.A: Trap: overstating. The writer says 'I am not saying we should throw away our phones.'
mistakes.B: Trap: inventing a complaint. The price of stamps is never mentioned.
mistakes.C: Trap: reversing a fact. The writer admits letters are slower and says that is the point.

questions.prompt: In Passage D, 'thank you, I'm sorry, I miss you' is an example of which persuasive technique?

options.A: A rhetorical question
options.B: A statistic
options.C: A quotation from an expert
options.D: A list of three examples

questions.explanation: Three short examples in a row form a 'rule of three' list, which sounds complete and memorable. None of the phrases is a question, so it isn't a rhetorical question.
steps: Count the items: 'thank you', 'I'm sorry', 'I miss you' — three.
Three items in a row form a list of three, used to make a point stick.
So the technique is a list of three examples.

mistakes.A: Trap: naming a device that isn't there. None of these phrases is a question.
mistakes.B: Trap: naming a device that isn't there. There are no numbers here.
mistakes.C: Trap: naming a device that isn't there. No expert is named or quoted.

questions.prompt: How does the writer of Passage D deal with the view that waiting is the worst thing about letters?

options.A: She agrees, and says this is why letters are not worth writing.
options.B: She ignores the idea and talks about something else.
options.C: She mentions what people say, then argues that waiting actually makes replies special.
options.D: She says the post is now so fast that there is really no waiting for a reply at all any more.

questions.explanation: 'People say this is the worst thing … but I disagree. Waiting … turns it into an event.' She names the opposing view and then turns it into a strength. She does not agree with it.
steps: Find the paragraph: 'People say this is the worst thing about letters, but I disagree.'
She then says waiting 'turns it into an event' and gives her cousin's letters as an example.
So she names the opposing view and argues waiting makes replies special.

mistakes.A: Trap: stopping after 'People say…'. The next words are 'but I disagree'.
mistakes.B: Trap: missing the paragraph. She spends a whole paragraph answering it.
mistakes.D: Trap: inventing a claim. She accepts there is waiting and says it is good.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer of Passage D mention her grandmother's crossed sevens and the coffee ring from her cousin?

options.A: To complain that her relatives are messy
options.B: To prove that her grandmother writes more letters, and longer ones, than her cousin in Darwin does
options.C: To show that handwritten letters carry personal details of the person who wrote them
options.D: To explain the right way to write the number seven

questions.explanation: The examples back up 'Handwriting carries a person in a way a screen font never can' — little personal marks a text message would not have. The tone is fond, not complaining.
steps: Find the sentence before the examples: 'Handwriting carries a person in a way a screen font never can.'
The crossed sevens and coffee ring are personal marks of the writers.
So they show that letters carry personal details of the sender.

mistakes.A: Trap: misjudging the tone. She mentions these lovingly as things she treasures.
mistakes.B: Trap: inventing a comparison. Nothing says who writes more.
mistakes.D: Trap: taking a detail literally. The sevens show her grandmother's personal style.

questions.prompt: In Passage D, 'A letter takes time to write, and that is exactly the point.' Here 'the point' means

options.A: the main reason or purpose
options.B: the sharp tip of a pen
options.C: a full stop at the end of a sentence
options.D: a score earned in a game

questions.explanation: The writer says the slowness of letters is the whole reason they are valuable — 'the point' means the purpose. The pen-tip meaning is tempting because pens appear in the passage, but it doesn't fit the sentence.
steps: Read the sentences after: taking time makes you 'think harder' and be 'more honest'.
So the slowness is the reason letters are worth writing.
'The point' means the main reason or purpose.

mistakes.B: Trap: a different meaning of 'point'. Pens are mentioned, but this sentence is about why letters matter.
mistakes.C: Trap: a different meaning. Nothing here is about punctuation.
mistakes.D: Trap: a different meaning. No game is involved.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer of Passage D say, 'I am not saying we should throw away our phones'?

options.A: To change her mind and argue against letters
options.B: To advertise a particular kind of phone
options.C: To seem fair and reasonable, which makes her argument easier to accept
options.D: To show readers that she does not own a phone herself and has never needed one

questions.explanation: By admitting phones are useful for quick messages, she avoids sounding extreme, so readers are more willing to agree with her main point. She still argues for letters, so she has not changed her mind.
steps: She admits phones are useful: 'I use mine every day'.
Admitting a fair point makes a writer sound reasonable, not extreme.
So she says it to seem fair, making her argument easier to accept.

mistakes.A: Trap: misreading a concession. She still ends by telling readers to write a letter.
mistakes.B: Trap: inventing a purpose. No brand or product is mentioned.
mistakes.D: Trap: contradicting the text. She says, 'I use mine every day.'

questions.prompt: Passage D ends: 'You might be surprised by what comes back.' This most likely suggests that

options.A: the letter might be returned because the address is wrong
options.B: the reader will receive a parcel instead of a letter
options.C: writing a letter may bring a meaningful reply and a closer connection
options.D: the writer expects the reader to be disappointed

questions.explanation: After praising how special replies are (her shoebox of letters), the ending hints that writing a letter can bring a reply and a stronger bond. A returned letter is the literal trap.
steps: Remember the passage values replies: waiting for one 'turns it into an event'.
'What comes back' means the reply — and the closeness it brings.
So it suggests a letter may bring a meaningful reply and a closer connection.

mistakes.A: Trap: reading it literally. The writer is talking about replies, not lost mail.
mistakes.B: Trap: inventing a detail. Nothing mentions parcels.
mistakes.D: Trap: missing the hopeful tone. 'Surprised' here is positive, after a passage praising letters.
